name: The Champion Paradise Tree of Simpson Park

location.address: Simpson Park, 55 SW 17th Road, Miami, FL 33129 (behind the Charles Torrey Simpson Garden Center building, near the park's main/east entrance)

access: Free. City of Miami park, open daily 8am-5pm (east entrance closes 4pm); closed on holidays.
transport: In the Brickell/The Roads neighbourhood just south of downtown Miami; no Metrorail station within easy walk, nearest is roughly a mile away. Reachable by Metrobus on nearby routes, bike, rideshare, or on foot from Brickell (about 20-25 minutes).
verify_notes: City of Miami's own 2022 Simpson Park brochure (official park map/guide, archived copy fetched because live miami.gov PDF returned Access Denied to curl) labels this specimen 'Paradise Tree (Champion Tree)' as stop on the park's numbered nature trail, located behind the Charles Torrey Simpson Garden Center building. floridahikes.com independently describes it as 'a large paradise tree behind the building designated as a National Champion tree... the largest known example of its species in the country', confirming the champion designation from a second, independent source. Simpson Park Hammock is a 7.8-acre remnant of the historic Brickell Hammock tropical hardwood forest, one of the last such fragments in urban Miami (Wikipedia: Simpson Park Hammock), so the setting itself is remarkable, not just this one tree. Champion status here is about SIZE (largest known of the species), not documented age; no age or girth figure found in either source, so left blank rather than guessed - Simarouba glauca is not typically a multi-century tree. Alive/current: brochure is dated 2022, five years after Hurricane Irma (2017) closed the park for canopy damage, so evidence of life postdates that storm; no more recent (2023+) dated confirmation found in this pass. Location is approximate: I have the park's centroid and the brochure's own trail map showing the tree's position relative to the Garden Center building and numbered stops, but no independent tree-level GPS coordinate, so a visitor should look for the marked nature-trail stop behind the Garden Center rather than trust the pin to the metre. Flagged for: (1) no independent dated (2023+) confirmation of survival, (2) no age data, (3) pin is park-level/building-relative, not tree-level. A visitor or park naturalist (contact in the brochure: Gloria Antia, Parks Naturalist Senior) could confirm current status and exact spot.

name: The Garden Mound Oaks of Vizcaya

location.address: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens, 3251 South Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33129 (the Garden Mound, an artificial hill near the south end of the formal gardens)

access: Paid entry to Vizcaya Museum and Gardens (general admission ticket required); open Wednesday-Monday, closed Tuesdays. The Garden Mound is a short walk from the main entrance, up a set of stone stairs.
transport: Vizcaya Metrorail station (on the Metrorail/M-Path) is about a 500m, 5-10 minute walk from the entrance.
verify_notes: Four Southern Live Oaks (Quercus virginiana) crown the Garden Mound, an artificial hill built during construction of Vizcaya (1914-1922) as the winter estate of James Deering. Vizcaya's own official interpretive label (vizcaya.org/gardenmound-label) calls them '200-year old, windswept Live Oak trees' and says the mound is one of the few spots where 'the house appears small, almost a miniature', with 360-degree views over the mangrove shore, the rockland hammock and the formal gardens. Independent source sofiascountrygardens.com corroborates the mechanism without repeating Vizcaya's own age claim: the four oaks were already mature specimens dug from another Deering-owned property and moved to the mound during construction, 'transplanted one hundred years ago' (from that source's own vantage point), which is consistent with (not identical to, so not treated as a bridge to a precise figure) Vizcaya's 200-year claim: mature at transplant circa 1914-1922 plus roughly a century since. Age is real estate PR language from the institution itself rather than an independent dendrological measurement, so flagged and given as a broad range (150-220y) rather than repeated as an exact 200. No girth recorded by either source. Deering deliberately imported large mature trees property-wide to fake an established look immediately (About Gardens page also documents a large strangler fig moved by barge that blew down in a storm, and over 100 Royal Palms shipped from Cuba, one surviving specimen recognised as a Florida Challenger, the fourth-largest Royal Palm in the state - a possible second entry for a later pass). Vizcaya's forest also holds 8 documented national champion trees per the same official page, unnamed in the source, worth a targeted follow-up. Alive now: the oaks are a maintained, actively promoted feature of a paying museum with a dedicated 2020s-era interpretive page about them, and are 'regularly trimmed... to be more resilient during storms' per vizcaya.org, so recent tending is documented even without a dated 2023+ photo. Location is approximate: pin is the Vizcaya property centroid: the Garden Mound itself sits toward the south end of the formal gardens near the water, findable on-site from the entrance via the garden map, but I do not have the mound's own coordinate.

name: David Fairchild's Inauguration Baobab

location.address: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden, 10901 Old Cutler Road, Coral Gables, FL 33156 (near the Sunken Garden, in the Montgomery Palmetum)

access: Paid entry to Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden (general admission ticket required); open daily.
transport: No Metrorail or Metrobus stop within easy walking distance; typically reached by car (parking on site).
verify_notes: Planted by the botanist Dr. David Fairchild himself at the Garden's public inauguration on 23 March 1938 (fairchildgarden.org's own 'Early Plantings' page, which is a documented planting record for THIS specific specimen, not a bridge from the garden's founding date), grown from material Fairchild collected on the 1927 Utowana expedition to West Africa. Wikipedia's Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden article independently confirms: 'Many plants still growing in the Garden were collected and planted by him [Fairchild], including a giant African baobab tree' - corroborating that this specific tree is (a) still alive and (b) one Fairchild personally planted, from a source outside the garden's own site. Species confirmed as Adansonia digitata (African baobab) by fairchildgarden.org. Note there is a SECOND, larger baobab elsewhere in the garden (near the Phillips-Atwater Gatehouse, also planted 1938 but from Dade County Nursery stock, not Fairchild's own expedition material) - do not conflate the two; this entry is specifically the Sunken Garden / Montgomery Palmetum specimen with the Fairchild-personal planting story, which is the more remarkable one. Age is a straightforward documented-planting-date calculation (2026 minus 1938), not an estimate, so it is unusually solid for this database, though as an ex-situ botanic-garden specimen its 'remarkable' quality is historical/horticultural (a named plant-hunter's own tree, still growing 88 years on) rather than ancient-age or huge-size. No girth or height found in either source. Alive now: it is a named, signed stop the garden itself still promotes on a page updated recently, so institutional maintenance implies current life, though no dated 2023+ photo or observation was found in this pass. Location is approximate: I have the garden's entrance/building coordinate plus the descriptive location ('near the Sunken Garden in the Montgomery Palmetum'), not a tree-level GPS pin; the garden's own map or a staff member on site could confirm the exact spot.
